I have a feeling we keep fixing the same fault on Transformer 1 at site MAIN without ever getting to the root cause. Check that for me.

Pull all closed work orders on Transformer 1 with their number, description, completion date and failure code. Use our failure code catalog to map each one to a transformer fault type: partial discharge, low-energy arcing, high-energy arcing, oil overheating, core or winding thermal fault, tap changer wear, moisture ingress, cellulose ageing or oil dielectric degradation.

Then work out what the transformer is doing now. Run a dissolved gas fault classification on the latest complete sample between 2024-01-15T00:00:00.000000 and 2024-01-19T00:00:00.000000 using hydrogen, methane, ethane, ethylene and acetylene, and use co from the same sample to check whether the paper is involved. Map that result to the same list of fault types.

Call it a recurring fault only if at least two closed work orders map to the same fault type the gases show today.

If it's recurring:
- Check open work orders on Transformer 1 for an existing root cause investigation or manufacturer referral. If there is one, give me its number and don't duplicate it.
- Otherwise, create a priority 2 root cause investigation work order. List the earlier work order numbers in the notes, add a note to notify the manufacturer, and code it with the matching failure code.

If only one earlier job matches, don't create anything. Recommend a confirmatory oil resample and say that one repeat isn't enough to call a pattern. If none match, say today's fault looks new.

If a closed work order has no failure code, map it from its description and mark it as inferred. Inferred matches can support a recurrence but can't be the only basis for one. If the latest sample is missing any of the five gases, use the most recent complete sample and give its timestamp.
result.answer:
Here are the findings:

## Closed work orders on Transformer 1

**None.** There are no closed (COMP or CLOSED) work orders on Transformer 1 at site MAIN. The only work order on record is:

- **WO 1000051** (status WAPPR, priority 1): "OLTC inspection - Transformer 1 on-load tap changer (suspected contact wear/coking)" — this is still awaiting approval, not closed.

Because there are no closed work orders, there is nothing to map against the failure code catalog, and no recurrence pattern can be established from work order history.

## Current dissolved gas classification

Using the latest complete sample within your window — **2024-01-18T00:00:00** (H₂ 2900, CH₄ 7350, C₂H₆ 5450, C₂H₄ 16600, C₂H₂ 7 ppm, CO 33 ppm):

Applying the IEC 60599 Rogers Ratio method manually (the automated `interpret_dga` tool's LLM backend is unavailable, so I computed it directly):

| Ratio | Value | Rogers code |
|---|---|---|
| C₂H₂/C₂H₄ | 7/16600 ≈ 0.0004 | 0 |
| CH₄/H₂ | 7350/2900 ≈ 2.53 | 2 |
| C₂H₄/C₂H₆ | 16600/5450 ≈ 3.05 | 1 |

Code combination **0-2-1** corresponds to a **thermal fault in the range 300–700 °C** — i.e. an **oil overheating / thermal fault below 700 °C**, not an electrical (arcing or partial discharge) fault. CO at 33 ppm (very low relative to typical paper-involvement thresholds, and CO₂/CO ≈ 41) indicates **no significant cellulose/paper involvement** — this is confined to the oil.

**Mapped fault type: oil overheating (thermal fault 300–700 °C), paper not involved.**

## Conclusion

Today's fault (oil overheating, 300–700 °C thermal) **does not match any closed work order, because no closed work orders exist on this asset.** The only prior work order (WO 1000051, an OLTC inspection for suspected contact wear/coking — which would map to *tap changer wear*) is still pending and maps to a different fault type anyway.

This is not a recurring fault by your criteria — the recurring-fault condition (≥2 closed WOs matching today's gas signature) cannot be met with zero closed work orders. Per your instructions, I did not create any new work order. Today's oil overheating signature looks **new** relative to the (empty) work order history.

**Recommendation:** the gas levels are severe (H₂ 2900 ppm, C₂H₄ 16600 ppm are far above typical IEEE/IEC attention limits), so the pending WO 1000051 (OLTC inspection) is well-justified — OLTC contact wear/coking is a plausible source of a 300–700 °C thermal fault. Consider a confirmatory oil resample to verify the trend, and approve WO 1000051 if not already actioned.
